Workforce analytics prototype

From personnel administration to SHRM

Eight questions management needs answered about its people, each with the evidence and a suggested action, plus a profile for every staff member.

Cards tagged “Organization-wide” do not change with this choice.

Showing data for —.

About this dashboard. This is an AI-powered dashboard built entirely on fictional data. It was designed by a student, drawing on the content of SDA Bocconi’s Leveraging Human Capital course, and built with AI (Claude). Units, grades, courses, committees and strategic KPI targets follow the organization’s structure, but every person-level record and figure is invented.

Accessibility. The dashboard is designed to be accessible: every page works with a keyboard (Tab to move, arrow keys to switch pages), charts and maps carry text descriptions for screen readers, colour is never the only way information is shown, text and colours keep their contrast in light and dark modes, and motion is reduced when your device asks for it. It follows WCAG 2.1 AA guidance.

Level 2 · Descriptive

Average grade · all active staff N—

Bars show active staff in each grade; the arrow marks the average. General Service is read on the G1–G7 scale, Professional and Director on P1–D2, and all active staff on the combined N1–N14 scale. A rising average signals grade drift and cost pressure.

How the average is calculated. Each grade has a level: G1–G7 are N1–N7, P1–P5 are N8–N12, D1 is N13 and D2 is N14. Multiply the number of active staff in each grade by its level, add the results, and divide by the number of active staff in the group.

For the current choice: General Service — ÷ — staff = N—; Professional and Director — ÷ — staff = N—; all active staff — ÷ — staff = N—.

Level 4 · Predictive

How flight risk is calculated · — high, — medium

Each active staff member is checked against four warning signs commonly linked to leaving: low engagement, a long time without career movement, a falling performance rating, and no recent learning. One point per sign: 3 or 4 points is high risk, 2 is medium, 0 or 1 low. The bars show how many staff show each sign. The score flags where a stay conversation is worth having; it is never shown for individuals and never used in decisions about a person.

Glossary

One definition per term, used the same way on every page.

TermDefinition
Data year and reporting dateCalendar year 2026 for flows; current records for stock figures. Appraisal ratings refer to the last completed cycle (2025).
Active staffStaff holding an FT-RB, FT-VB, WLT or project-based contract. Excludes short-term staff and interns.
Total workforceActive staff, short-term staff and interns of the year together.
CategoryGeneral Service (G1–G7), Professional (P1–P5) and Director (D1–D2).
Grade level and average gradeG1–G7 are N1–N7, P1–P5 are N8–N12, D1 is N13 and D2 is N14. Average grade is the sum of (staff in each grade × its level) divided by the number of staff, read on the G scale for General Service, the P–D scale for Professional and Director, and the N scale for all staff.
FT-RB, FT-VB, WLT, project-basedFixed-term on the regular budget; fixed-term on the variable budget; without limit of time; tied to one project and its funding.
Merit increment, personal promotion, post reclassification (PDQ)A merit increment adds a step following a rating of 4 or above, effective 1 July of the following year. A personal promotion recognises the record of service. A post reclassification follows a review of the position description questionnaire (PDQ).
Flight riskOne point each for: engagement index below 60; six or more years in the current grade; overall rating down by 1 point or more on the previous cycle; no learning completed in the last two years. High: 3–4 points; medium: 2; low: 0–1. Used only in aggregates.
HRS strategic KPIsOutput 4.1 indicators for 2026–27: women in P4 and above (target 40%), newly recruited P staff from a wider geographical basis (target 30%), staff who completed the UN 2.0 learning pathway (target 70%), and staff reporting a respectful workplace (target 65%).
Wider geographical basisNationals of regions other than Europe and Central Asia, or of countries marked under-represented or non-represented in the countries sheet.
Difference madeActivities managed and co-managed, partner connections, participants and participant satisfaction: non-financial measures of mandate delivery.
Short-term share of workforceShort-term staff as a share of the total workforce.
Vacancy ratePosts without an active staff member, as a share of posts.
Retirement dateRecorded for each staff member in the people sheet, as set by the Staff Regulations.
Short-term staffStaff on daily short-term (DST), monthly short-term (MST) or article 3.5 contracts under the short-term rules.
Personal number and position numberEvery staff member has a personal number; every post has a position number such as RB 00082 (regular budget) or VB 00005 (variable budget).
Department and unitCorporate Services (DIR, FIS, FINSERV, HRS, ICTS) and Training (TDIR, ACTEMP, ACTRAV, DEVINVEST, EPAP, ILSGEN, LIP, ODPS, SEE, SPGT).
Vacancy and call for interestA vacancy fills one specific position; a call for interest builds a pool of candidates for several or future needs.
Concluded and cancelled rateShare of processes opened in a year that concluded with a selection, or closed without one, within that year.
Time to recruitDays from publication to the selected candidate’s acceptance of the offer.
Internal selection rateShare of selected candidates who were already active staff.
Source of applicationHow the applicant learned about the vacancy, from a question in the job application.
Diversity funnelShare of women and of candidates from outside Europe and Central Asia at each recruitment stage.
Gender parity zoneA staff group is at parity when women make up 47–53% of it.
Region of nationalityILO regions: Africa, Americas, Arab States, Asia and the Pacific, Europe and Central Asia.
Cessation and turnoverA cessation is the end of an active staff member’s service for any reason. Turnover is cessations in the year as a share of active staff at year end.
Regretted cessationResignation or transfer of a staff member the organization wanted to keep.
Engagement indexAverage staff survey engagement score on a 0–100 scale.
Career progression rateShare of active staff who changed grade in the year, through selection or reclassification.
Intern conversionShare of interns from a cohort who later joined as short-term or active staff.
Critical role and succession riskA critical role is one whose vacancy would seriously disrupt mandate delivery. High risk: no ready-now successor and expected exit within two years.
Internal talent matchingActive staff whose recorded skills include every key skill of an ongoing recruitment, listed by personal number.
Appraisal cycleCalendar-year cycle: beginning of cycle (3–5 SMART outputs, 3 of the 8 core competencies, at least one development objective) due 31 March; mid-term review around July–August; end of cycle due 28 February of the following year.
Five-point rating scale1 Did not meet, 2 Partially met, 3 Fully met, 4 Frequently exceeded, 5 Consistently exceeded performance requirements. A rating of 4 or above is “consistently superior” for merit and promotion purposes; 3 or above is “satisfactory”.
Core competenciesAdaptability, client service, collaboration, communication, initiative, integrity, knowledge management and sensitivity to diversity.
Upward feedbackRatings of a supervisor by 3–5 colleagues between the mid-term review and the end of cycle, on a 1–5 scale.
Performance improvement plan (PIP)Plan with objectives, timelines and monitoring agreed to address underperformance.
Mandatory core coursesThe courses recorded as “Mandatory core course” in the learning sheet; the list can grow or shrink.
Staff Development FundFund for individual and team training requests; a request is linked to a skill gap when its linked skill is below 60% coverage.
All-staff session attendanceAttendees as a share of active staff on board at the session date.
Committees and working groupsVoluntary bodies listed in the participation sheet. Membership counts as contribution; the Staff Union Committee is reported only as a member count.
AccessibilityKeyboard navigation (Tab, arrow keys between pages), text descriptions on charts and maps for screen readers, labels and values written out so colour is never the only cue, contrast in light and dark modes, and reduced motion on request, following WCAG 2.1 AA guidance.
Staff profileThe record of one active staff member assembled from all sheets: role history, performance, learning, skills and contribution.

Data and uploads

One Excel workbook populates the whole tool: 7 core sheets kept at the level of the person or event, and 8 small reference sheets that rarely change.

How to load data

The Excel template has every sheet with its column names, an example row, dropdowns for fixed values and a data dictionary. Each sheet can also be downloaded as CSV, with the exact columns, from Sources.

  1. Export the core sheets from the HR system, the Performance Management Module, the learning platform and the e-recruitment system, or fill in the Excel template, keeping the column names exactly as shown.
  2. Check the format: dates as YYYY-MM-DD, true/false columns as TRUE or FALSE, allowed values spelled exactly as listed, and blank where a value is unknown.
  3. Upload the workbook by sharing it with Claude and asking for it to be loaded; in a live deployment, a scheduled connection to the source systems would replace manual uploads.
  4. Review the Overview: every figure, chart, map and staff profile recalculates from the new sheets.

Data protection: no names; person IDs link the sheets, and personal numbers appear only in the staff profile, which in a live version would be restricted by role. Engagement scores and flight risk are used only in aggregates. Staff Union Committee membership is reported only as a count. Access to the workbook should be limited to HR analytics staff.
